---
title: "Agentic data-vis workshops"
---

Occasional, hands-on workshops on data visualisation with an **agentic AI assistant**,
grounded in Wilkinson's **grammar of graphics**. The work is mainly in R with ggplot2,
with excursions into Vega-Lite and plotnine to show the grammar moving between languages.
Each session takes one [TidyTuesday](https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday) (or
equivalent) dataset and builds a visualisation live. **Every design decision is made by
the people in the room.** The agent fetches and describes the data, writes the code,
renders the result, and reports what it sees.

There's no fixed schedule. Sessions happen when someone offers to run one, and the repo
is public so that anyone can: clone it, open it in an IDE with Claude Code, Codex, or
another coding agent, and the same skills and instructions apply. Started by
[Jon Minton](https://jonminton.net/).

## How the sessions work

Plots are specified before they are coded. The group dictates **mapping rules**: which
variable goes to which aesthetic, which geoms, which scales. These are recorded in a
short YAML spec that the group argues over on the shared screen, then compiled to code
and rendered. The spec trail *is* the record of the design decisions.
**[See a worked example of the round trip](example-gg-spec.qmd).**

For anyone who would rather point and click than write YAML, the
**[mapping builder](mapping-builder.qmd)** lets you draw the same mapping rules as arrows
from variables to aesthetics. It shows the figure, the spec and the ggplot2 code updating
together.

The opposite of "the analyst decides" is an agent that decides everything: the dataset,
the question and every figure. That is the
[claude-fable-vision-ds-test experiment](https://jonminton.github.io/claude-fable-vision-ds-test/)
([repository](https://github.com/JonMinton/claude-fable-vision-ds-test)), which these
workshops use as a point of contrast. Its
[probability-phrases page](https://jonminton.github.io/claude-fable-vision-ds-test/probability-phrases.html)
covers one of the datasets offered in Session 1.

The repo gives the agent three skills, each a plain-markdown procedure that any agent
can follow:

- **tt-fetch** fetches a TidyTuesday week and describes it in grammar terms. It
  *proposes* mappings and never chooses one.
- **gg-spec** compiles a YAML spec to ggplot2, renders it, and looks at the result. It
  walks the grammar one slot at a time, so the room makes each decision.
- **dataset-scout** finds datasets that stress a particular grammar layer, for planning
  a session.

After a session, a page may be drafted from the spec trail and notes, recording the
design decisions *as decisions*, the pain points, and the lessons learned. The session's
facilitator reviews and approves it before it is published.

## Consent and authorship

The Chatham House Rule applies by default: write-ups never attribute a view or a mistake
to an individual. Participants who consent may be **named** as contributors, which needs a
per-session consent record: no record, no name. Recordings and transcripts, if any, are
never published.

## Sessions

- **2026-09-29, a demonstration at a university data-vis lab.**
  [Slides](slides/2026-09-29-vishub.qmd). The room chose *The Office*: IMDb ratings for
  every episode, built into a season-by-episode heatmap and then ratings over air date.
  [The session workbook](sessions/2026-09-29/office-data.qmd), and
  [version 2](sessions/2026-09-29/office-data-v2.qmd), which continues it after the session.
  Version 2 adds revised specs, a 3D view with explicit linear models, and an
  autonomously produced section on the transcripts.
